There’s a flash of red down the road. We’ve already been driving for hours through the Peruvian Amazon and, at first, I think my bleary eyes are deceiving me. But as we crawl further down this long dirt strip — flanked by pineapple fields dotted with straw-hatted workers — a woman appears, her crimson dress looking like a burning flame. As we approach, I notice a cascade of necklaces across her chest. Around her waist, a belt adorned with snail shells — strung vertically like a beaded curtain — clinks and clacks as she extends her arms in greeting. “Welcome to the Nuwas Forest,” she says in Spanish. This is Margarita Cumbia Sawao. She’s an elder of the local Awajún community, whose women have become custodians of this once-threatened area of the rainforest. pages.text: Meet the Marseille Chefs Championing Bouillabaisse, France's Favorite Fish Dish | National Geographic TRAVEL Meet the Marseille Chefs Championing Bouillabaisse, France's Favorite Fish Dish The classic fish soup was born in France’s vibrant port city, where the most feted versions can still be found — alongside some inspired innovations. The bouillabaisse at Bar des Goudes was named as the world's best in the Bouillabaisse World Championship. Jonathan Stokes By Sarah Barrell Published October 28, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). “People thought we were crazy when we first served this,” says Linda Vila Palleja, handing me what is effectively a soup sandwich from behind a counter. “But each bite delivers all flavours at once. You know you’re eating bouillabaisse.” She’s not wrong. The delicate, almost smoky softness of the broth-poached fish — today it’s red gurnard but Linda and her husband Hervé cook whatever’s fresh — is encased in a baguette, lightly toasted for a crouton-like crunch. I dress mine with scoops from pots of rust-coloured fish broth — rich with tomatoes and aromatic vegetables, saffron and Med’ herbs — and garlicky-piquant saffron rouille . It’s a perfect serving of France’s definitive fish soup, in sandwich form. “Now, people thank me,” says Linda, eyes sparkling under heavy-rimmed glasses. “They say we’re flying the flag for Marseille.” This generously stacked sandwich is an irreverently unorthodox rendering of the ancient fish soup-stew, born in the Provençal port city as a medieval fisherman’s supper. The first Arab mission to another planet, the Al Amal, or “Hope,” probe will capture the first comprehensive picture of the Martian climate. Thanks to its around-the-clock monitoring, the global science community will have the opportunity to study the relationship between Mars' current and ancient climates and investigate how atmospheres change over time. Almost as impressive as humanity's ability to send a probe 37 million miles to Mars and the unprecedented data that this mission will collect is the fact that the woman spearheading the scientific mission on this project, Her Excellency Sarah Al Amiri, has barely embarked on her 30s. The Hiligaynon language of the central Philippines is filled with mouthwatering onomatopoeia. There’s lagting (scraping and tapping cutlery), tamsak (smacking lips) and harakhak (cackling laughter). But the word that comes to mind as I tuck in to a brioche bun filled with ginamos , a pungent paste made from fish or shrimps, is mananam (umami). It’s based on the sound one makes when eating something delicious, and spills out as soon as I finish my meal — to the delight of Ramon ‘Chinchin’ Uy Jr, owner of organic restaurant Lanai by Fresh Start. pages.text: Meet the Salak, the Ubiquitous Indonesian Fruit You’ve Never Heard Of Skip to main content Monsaro’s snakefruit, freshly plucked from a nearby village. Photo by Rachel Nuwer At a morning market in Bali, the usual gaudy suspects – papayas, mangos, dragon fruit and heaps of rancid-smelling durians - are on display. For Western visitors seeking culinary novelty, however, the most enticing fruit likely will not be the biggest or the brightest, but a humble, shiny brown offering called the salak. For the uninitiated, this fleshy, spongey morsel offers a perfumed cocktail of bright flavors, with hints of pineapple, citrus, honey and possibly even soap. In Indonesia, salaks are as common as apples or oranges in the U.S. Also called snakefruit, this strawberry-sized, fig-shaped fruit comes encased in vivid, nutty-brown scales, not unlike that of a cobra or python. Heaps of salaks turn up daily at countless local markets, while touristy hotels offer them up in breakfast buffet lines as examples of typical island fare. The odd but ubiquitous morsels can be boiled with sugar into a sweet spread , pickled , vacuum dried and fried into chips or paired with other fruits and nuts , but locals prefer them best raw and straight off the tree. Freshwater crabs of the species ( Potamon fluviatile ) inhabit burrows in rivers and streams across Italy (one shown in Tuscany). Photograph By Emanuele Biggi Overwhelmed by the crabs, archaeologists hauled buckets of them out of the earth during excavations. Known scientifically as Potamon fluviatile , these crustaceans are the only large freshwater crabs indigenous to Italy. Researchers suspect that the population’s heritage is ancient, dating back to when Rome wasn’t much more than a marshy valley. ( Two Vampire Crab Species Found, Are Already Popular Pets) The crustaceans have not been extensively studied and have been largely forgotten about over the last 15 years. These crabs may have seen empires rise and fall, but new monitoring data suggest that this once plentiful population could be at risk of disappearing. pages.text: Melissa Aldana and Gonzalo Rubalcaba talk jazz : Alt.Latino : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Melissa Aldana and Gonzalo Rubalcaba talk jazz : Alt.Latino Jazz has often been called America's musical gift to the world. This week's guests remind us not only of the well-documented ways that Cuba revolutionized that gift, but also how it blossomed in South America. Chilean tenor saxophonist Melissa Aldana and Cuban pianist Gonzalo Rubalcaba stopped by after their recent Tiny Desk performance to chat about their own personal histories with jazz and its lineage in their respective countries. The memories Rubalcaba shares about Havana's jazz scene in the 1980s adds another layer to a story we've talked a lot about on Alt.Latino. And Aldana looks back on her youth learning music from her father and grandfather, both of whom were Chilean jazz pioneers. The conversation also covers the music they played at the Tiny Desk, which comes from their recent album, 'Filin,' a reexamination of a Cuban musical movement that lasted from the 1940s through the '60s. Ultimately, this week's episode is time spent with two master musicians to hear how their lives and experiences contribute to their mutual appreciation and love of jazz. pages.description: As climate change warms the planet, more discoveries of human remains and objects in ice are expected to occur
pages.text: Melting Swiss Glacier Reveals Remains of Climber Who Disappeared in 1986 Skip to main content Mountaineers came upon the gear and remains of a hiker missing since 1986 last month. Cantonal Police of Valais Mountaineers trekking along a glacier in Switzerland have made a surprising discovery: the body and equipment of a hiker who had been missing for nearly 40 years. On July 12, the group was traveling across Theodul Glacier in Zermatt, Switzerland, not far from the famous Matterhorn mountain, when they stumbled upon pieces of gear and human remains, per a statement from the local police. Authorities sent the remains for DNA testing at Valais Hospital, which revealed that the newly discovered body belonged to a German mountain climber who had gone missing in September 1986. The police did not share the deceased individual’s name, but they said the mountaineer was 38 years old in 1986. At the time, search teams tried to find the hiker but were ultimately unsuccessful. It’s not clear how or why the German alpinist died, nor the conditions that made it impossible for the person to return home safely. However, discoveries like this one may become more and more common amid rising global temperatures, as glaciers like Theodul continue to melt. “The retreat of the glaciers brings to light an increasing number of missing alpinists who were reported missing several decades ago,” police said in the statement. pages.text: Members Curator's Tour: Monet | Tate Modern Join curator Genevieve Barton for a Private View Curator's Tour of this major exhibition Take advantage of this exclusive Members Private View Curator's Tour and join Genevieve Barton, Assistant Curator, International Art for a one hour tour through this major exhibition. Tate Modern’s first ever exhibition focusing exclusively on Claude Monet brings together breathtaking paintings from lenders across the globe, including rarely seen works from private collections. The exhibition centres on Monet’s profound and evolving relationship with time. We see how he echoed the rapid pace of modern life by capturing the fleeting, instantaneous ‘impressionist’ moment, through works such as Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare (1877). We are also shown, in celebrated series such as Poplars on the Epte (1891–1897), Monet’s attempts, through variations of the same subject, to capture a specific, transient instant in time. Finally, the show reveals Monet’s enduring relationship with nature and how, as a subject in perpetual movement, it shifts with the passing years and seasons. We see his retreat into his beloved garden in Giverny, resulting in the creation of the world-famous Water Lilies cycle. Monet: Painting Time is supported by Lead Supporter, Morgan Stanley. pages.text: Members of the Court | INTERNATIONAL COURT OF JUSTICE Skip to main content Members of the Court The International Court of Justice is composed of 15 judges elected to nine-year terms of office by the United Nations General Assembly and the Security Council. These organs vote simultaneously but separately. In order to be elected, a candidate must receive an absolute majority of the votes in both bodies. This sometimes makes it necessary for a number of rounds of voting to be held. In order to ensure a degree of continuity, one third of the Court is elected every three years. Judges are eligible for re-election. Should a judge die or resign during his or her term of office, a special election is held as soon as possible to choose a judge to fill the unexpired part of the term. Elections are held in New York (United States of America) during the annual autumn session of the General Assembly. The judges elected at a triennial election commence their term of office on 6 February of the following year, after which the Court holds a secret ballot to elect a President and a Vice-President to hold office for three years. All States parties to the Statute of the Court have the right to propose candidates. Such proposals are made not by the government of the State concerned, but by a group consisting of the members of the Permanent Court of Arbitration (see History) designated by that State, i.e. by the four jurists who can be called upon to serve as members of an arbitral tribunal under the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907. pages.text: Membres de la Cour | COUR INTERNATIONALE DE JUSTICE Aller au contenu principal Membres de la Cour La Cour internationale de Justice se compose de quinze juges élus pour un mandat de neuf ans par l’Assemblée générale et le Conseil de sécurité des Nations Unies. Ces deux organes votent en même temps, mais dans des locaux séparés. Pour être déclaré élu, un candidat doit avoir obtenu la majorité absolue dans l’un et l’autre des organes, ce qui requiert parfois plusieurs tours de scrutin. En vue d’assurer une certaine continuité, la Cour est renouvelable par tiers tous les trois ans. Les juges sont rééligibles. Si un juge décède ou démissionne pendant son mandat, il est procédé dès que possible à une élection complémentaire pour la durée restant à courir. Les élections ont lieu à New York (États-Unis d’Amérique) à l’occasion de la session annuelle d’automne de l’Assemblée générale. Les nouveaux membres de la Cour entrent en fonctions le 6 février de l’année suivant leur élection, après quoi la Cour se choisit au scrutin secret un président et un vice-président pour les trois années suivantes. Le droit de proposer des candidats appartient à tous les États parties au Statut de la Cour. Dans chacun d’entre eux, les présentations sont faites non par le gouvernement mais par le groupe des membres de la Cour permanente d’arbitrage (voir «Historique») - c’est-à-dire par les quatre jurisconsultes susceptibles d’être appelés à faire partie d’un tribunal arbitral dans le cadre des conventions de La Haye de 1899 et de 1907 - ou, pour les pays non représentés à la Cour permanente d’arbitrag

Getting vaccinated and taking antibiotics offers some (but not complete) protection. People receiving complement inhibitors should seek treatment quickly for symptoms of meningococcal disease. Be aware that prompt treatment is important even for those who've been vaccinated or who are taking antibiotics. Meningococcal Disease in Other Countries Mar. 16, 2026 Key points Meningococcal disease occurs worldwide. The highest incidence of meningococcal disease is found in the 'meningitis belt' of sub-Saharan Africa. Other regions of the world experience lower overall rates of disease and occasional outbreaks. Learn about global trends in meningococcal disease. Meningitis belt The meningitis belt of sub-Saharan African historically experienced major epidemics of meningococcal disease every 5 to 12 years. Attack rates during these epidemics reached up to 1,000 cases per 100,000 population. Risk factors for meningococcal disease outbreaks in Africa aren't fully understood. Meningococcal Disease Symptoms and Complications Mar. 6, 2026 Español Key points Meningitis and bloodstream infections are the two most common types of meningococcal infections. Both are serious and can be deadly in a matter of hours. Symptoms of meningococcal disease can first appear as a flu-like illness and rapidly worsen. Seek medical attention immediately for symptoms of meningococcal disease. Symptoms Fever, stiff neck, and headache are common meningitis symptoms. pages.text: Menorca’s ‘houses of the dead’ reveal these ancient secrets | National Geographic By Eva van den Berg Published July 28, 2022 • 15 min read From atop Menorca’s megalithic stone towers, watchers would have witnessed the tides of history roll across the island with the successive waves of the ancient Mediterranean superpowers—the Phoenicians, Greeks, and Romans. But long before those heavyweights stepped ashore, the island’s humble pioneers carved out a life on the windswept, largely treeless landscape. Those towers, called talayots , were built from the raw material those first inhabitants and their descendants found in abundance—blocks of limestone. By simply making do with what they had, the Menorcans created a legacy set in stone. To most, Spain ’s Balearic Islands may be better known for the jet-set beach destinations of Ibiza and Mallorca. But tranquil Menorca, the easternmost link in the chain, combines that natural beauty with a unique treasure trove—the archipelago’s greatest repository of ancient architecture. Within these towers and other “ cyclopean ” structures—made from unhewn, mortarless stones—lies an island history knit together over a millennium, leaving its mark on the Menorcan landscape and identity. Menorca is home to almost 400 talayots, towers for which the Talayotic culture is named. Researchers believe the structures were probably used as watch towers or for defense, though their function is still subject to debate. Clean, lockable and reliable sanitation services – alongside safe water and hygiene facilities – are a source of protection and empowerment. But across continents, unsafe or absent toilet facilities expose hundreds of millions of women and girls to risks ranging from loss of privacy to assault. They can even discourage women from eating and drinking throughout the day and make menstruation harder to manage. These challenges restrict women and girls’ participation in public life, from schools and workplaces to civic spaces. That is why a community without effective sanitation can never achieve gender equality. Women, girls and other vulnerable groups must be able to participate in shaping solutions and managing services that meet everyone’s needs. This World Toilet Day, let us redouble our efforts to ensure toilets are accessible and safe, and accelerate progress towards a more equal future for all. Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s. At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989. The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's. These cartels control vast areas of the country and are also responsible for political corruption, assassinations and kidnappings. But which groups are the most powerful? The Sinaloa Cartel Territory: Much of the north-west. The US government has described the Sinaloa Cartel as one of the largest drug-trafficking organisations in the world. Founded in the late 1980s, it was for many years headed by the notorious drug lord Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán. "El Chapo" - or "Shorty" - was once ranked as one of the world's richest men. His life and vast drug-trafficking empire have been the subject of numerous books and TV series. Under his leadership, the cartel garnered a fierce reputation for violence and outfought several rival groups. Mexican cartels often clash with one another, but it's also worth noting that they can form strategic alliances as well. The Sinaloa became the biggest supplier of illegal drugs to the US during Guzmán's long reign as leader, officials say. pages.text: Mexico drugs: How one DEA killing began a brutal war - BBC News Image caption, The capture and murder of Enrique "Kiki" Camarena was a brazen moment in the drug war By Will Grant BBC News, Guadalajara Twenty seven years ago, the kidnap, torture and murder of a US Drug Enforcement Administration agent by Mexican drug traffickers sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America. It also offered an ominous warning of things to come. The picturesque Mexican city of Guadalajara is bustling with life. By day, its busy plazas are filled with street vendors and shoeshine boys. At night, the mariachis line up to play for the tourists. The country's drug violence feels very far from here and, most of the time, it is. But that was not always the case. "In 1985, Guadalajara was the base of operations for most of the major narcotics traffickers in North America," says James Kuykendall, then-head of the Guadalajara office of the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). "Many of the major traffickers from other parts of Mexico, especially the state of Sinaloa, had migrated to Guadalajara both for the scenery and for the politics: if they didn't have full immunity, certainly no-one was messing with them down there." Among the agents working out of the small office was a 37-year-old Mexican-born American, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena. César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year. The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers. Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations. The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday. A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports. pages.text: Mexico's Bread of the Dead Kneads Together Indigenous and Catholic Traditions Skip to main content Travel | October 30, 2026 Mexico’s Bread of the Dead Kneads Together Indigenous and Catholic Traditions Pan de Muerto, a Mexican sweet bread eaten for Día de los Muertos, is more than just a festive treat. Its history mirrors the holiday itself, a combination of cultures that breathes life back into the dead Pan de muerto is an orange-scented sweet bread traditionally prepared and eaten during Día de los Muertos , a Mexican holiday celebrated each year from October 31 to November 2. Eder Marcos Camacho Gomez/Getty Images Pan de muerto is an orange-scented sweet bread traditionally prepared and eaten during Día de los Muertos , a Mexican holiday celebrated each year from October 31 to November 2. Eder Marcos Camacho Gomez/Getty Images It’s autumn in Mexico City, and baker Elena Reygadas and her team at Panadería Rosetta are hard at work in the kitchen. Deftly, they shape mounds of soft, elastic dough into perfect rounds. Then, with two fingers, they gingerly form the huesitos , or little bones, laying the thin strips in a cross over the buns. A tray full of rolls slides into the bakery rack, resting alongside dozens of other matching loaves waiting for their turn in the oven. The bakers are making pan de muerto , an orange-scented sweet bread traditionally prepared and eaten during Día de los Muertos , Day of the Dead, a Mexican holiday celebrated each year from October 31 to November 2. For three days, legend decrees, the border between the mortal and spirit realms disappears.

Key takeaways An MFA is a graduate degree program focused on your chosen discipline within the arts, such as creative writing, studio art, or theater. The average cost of a master’s degree ranges from $44,640 to $71,640 [ 1 ]. MFA degree programs are generally structured as either low-residency or high-residency programs. Popular MFA concentrations include visual arts, performing arts, design, and creative writing. You can earn your MFA either in person or online , depending on the university and program you choose. Learn about the areas where you can earn an MFA, the benefits of attending an MFA program, and the salaries you may achieve after graduation. What is an MFA degree? An MFA is a master’s degree focusing on coursework in a specific artistic field, such as visual arts, performing arts, creative writing, or design. Many people consider MFAs as terminal degrees , meaning that you can earn the highest degree in that subject matter. As such, the degree often qualifies you to teach at the university level and to pursue other opportunities related to your field. It is now permanently closed . For the first time, MI5’s history was on display to the public, made possible through an unprecedented partnership between the Security Service and The National Archives. Visitors explored the ever-changing world of espionage and security threats through original case files, photographs and papers, alongside the real equipment used by spies and spy-catchers over MI5’s 115-year history. Ciamarra heads the Office of Policy and Rulemaking (APL) where he will advise the Administrator on major policy questions, lead the development of the FAA’s policy agenda, lead rulemaking and deregulatory efforts, and oversee the FAA’s implementation of congressional reauthorization. APL drives the agency’s strategic planning and national aviation policy – including environmental and energy strategy, aviation activity forecasts, and economic analyses. Ciamarra came to the FAA from Southwest Airlines where he was Senior Federal Affairs Director. There he developed the federal legislative and regulatory strategy for the company on issues such as air traffic control, airport development, and transportation security.
